title: Efficient and accurate steering of large language models through attention-guided feature learning
abstract: Activation steering, or direct manipulation of internal activations to guide large language model (LLM) responses toward specific semantic concepts, is emerging as a promising avenue for both understanding how semantic concepts are stored within LLMs and advancing LLM capabilities. Yet, existing steering methods are remarkably brittle, with seemingly nonsteerable concepts becoming completely steerable based on subtle algorithmic choices in how concept-related features are extracted. In this work, we introduce an attention-guided framework for activation steering that overcomes three core challenges associated with steering: 1) automatic selection of relevant token embeddings for extracting concept-related features; 2) accounting for heterogeneity of concept-related features across LLM activations; and 3) identification of layers most relevant for steering. Across a steering benchmark of 512 semantic concepts, our framework substantially improved steering over previous state-of-the-art (nearly doubling the number of successfully steered concepts) across model architectures and sizes (up to 70 billion parameter models). Furthermore, we use our framework to shed light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers. Overall, our framework opens further avenues for developing efficient, highly scalable fine-tuning algorithms for industry-scale LLMs.

title: Metaheuristic and Nonlinear Optimization for Intelligent Energy and Environmental Systems: A Review of Renewable Generation, Smart Metering, Networks and Environmental Monitoring
abstract: Energy and environmental systems are full of decisions that must be tuned under uncertainty: how much power to draw from a solar panel, how to bill and balance consumption on a smart grid, how to share spectrum in a wireless network and how to read a biosensor in the field. Computing itself is part of the problem, since data centres, web services and smartphones draw a growing share of electricity. Many of these decisions have no closed-form solution because the underlying models are nonlinear, noisy or only partly known. Metaheuristic search, fuzzy reasoning, nonlinear analysis and data-driven forecasting are now used to find good settings, but studies are spread across power engineering, networking and environmental science. This chapter reviews optimization and learning methods for five groups of problems: renewable generation and grid interfacing, smart metering and energy forecasting, resource allocation and energy-aware computing in communication and IoT systems, environmental and agricultural monitoring, and the approximation of nonlinear physical models. The review finds that hybrid metaheuristics, such as grey wolf optimization with opposition-based learning, improve tracking and control in renewable systems, that tree ensembles and regression models are standard for consumption forecasting, that fuzzy optimization handles uncertainty in network resource allocation, that signal-aware transfer scheduling and green design guidelines reduce the energy used by smartphones and web services, and that neural approximation can stand in for expensive solvers of nonlinear equations. Few studies, however, compare methods on shared benchmarks or report computation cost. Future work should use common test systems, report run time next to solution quality and link optimization with forecasting in one loop.

title: DEA-Leak and DEA ArtifactGuard 2.0: Public-Safe Reproducibility Package
abstract: DEA-Leak / DEA ArtifactGuard 2.0 — Public-Safe Reproducibility Package DEA ArtifactGuard 2.0 is an open-source research software package accompanying the manuscript DEA-Leak: Post-Computation Record Reconstruction and Automated Release Hardening for Data Envelopment Analysis. The software investigates privacy leakage arising from the disclosure of Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) result artifacts, including efficiency scores, peer intensities (lambda coefficients), input and output slacks, and projected target coordinates. For radial CCR and BCC models, the framework identifies algebraic reconstruction paths through which combinations of released analytical outputs may reveal confidential decision-making unit (DMU) input and output values. DEA ArtifactGuard 2.0 provides coordinate-level disclosure analysis, automated reconstruction-path detection, release-schema auditing, and minimum-declared-utility-loss artifact suppression for configurable protection levels. The reproducibility package includes: Python source code and command-line interface. Deterministic synthetic reconstruction experiments. Coordinate-granular reconstruction validation across CCR/BCC model families and input/output orientations. Exhaustive release-artifact subset auditing. Optimization validation against brute-force reference solutions. Native software verification records involving the R packages Benchmarking and deaR. Automated tests and reproducibility documentation. The public validation suite includes 20 synthetic dataset-model cases, exhaustive enumeration of 128 release subsets per orientation, and 144 optimizer-versus-brute-force validation instances. Data availability: The confidential KOSGEB firm-level administrative dataset and KOSGEB-derived numerical result files are not included in this public archive. Security limitations: DEA ArtifactGuard 2.0 addresses explicitly modeled DEA reconstruction paths. It does not provide differential privacy, cryptographic confidentiality, or protection against all possible inference attacks. Source code: https://github.com/huseyinsen1/DEA-Leak-ArtifactGuard Software version: 2.0.0 License: MIT

title: A Lifelong Neuro-Symbolic Explainable AI Twin for Zero-Touch 6G IoE Management Under Non-Stationary Network Dynamics
abstract: Future sixth-generation (6G) Internet of Everything (IoE) networks require zero-touch management systems capable of autonomously allocating communication and computational resources, satisfying service-level constraints, and providing transparent explanations for their decisions. Existing neuro-symbolic explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) twins improve interpretability by coupling neural prediction with symbolic reasoning; however, most rely on statically engineered causal graphs, fixed rule sets, and immutable knowledge bases. Such closed-world assumptions are unsuitable for non-stationary 6G environments in which radio conditions, mobility patterns, interference relationships, and service requirements continuously evolve. To address this limitation, this paper proposes LL-NS-XAI, a Lifelong Learning Neuro-Symbolic XAI Digital Twin for zero-touch 6G IoE management. The framework integrates three tightly coupled planes: an online implicit learner at the physical edge for time-varying service association and uplink/downlink resource allocation; a dynamic explicit learner in the virtual core for directed acyclic graph (DAG)-based Bayesian reasoning, most-probable-explanation inference, and explainable trust scoring; and a meta-cognitive layer that monitors reasoning residuals, detects parameter drift, structural drift, and ontological emergence, and autonomously revises the causal graph, probabilistic rule sets, conditional probability tables, and knowledge base. Unlike static neuro-symbolic twins, LL-NS-XAI treats realized post-decision outcomes, including achieved channel quality indicator (CQI), measured end-to-end delay, and throughput, as interventional evidence for online causal-model adaptation. Experimental evaluation using a non-stationary 5G-derived dataset with injected parameter drift, structural drift, and emergent IoE service classes demonstrates that LL-NS-XAI maintains higher long-term trustworthiness, lower reasoning residuals, and bounded performance degradation compared with static XAI twins, non-stationary bandits, and pure continual-learning baselines. The framework additionally accommodates a previously unseen IoE service class through autonomous causal-graph expansion, recovering near-oracle performance without offline retraining. These results demonstrate that lifelong causal adaptation can improve the robustness, explainability, and autonomy of AI-enabled zero-touch management in evolving 6G IoE networks.

title: Self-Building Labs
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still takes extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting the role of human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable. Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/

title: QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality-Diversity
abstract: Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to recommendation for decision-making, focusing on decisions where the set of possible choices is fixed but the reasons for choosing them are not. In high-stakes decisions, e.g., which company to acquire or which customer to target, comparing diverse, well-reasoned options can be more useful than a single ranked list. We formalize open-ended recommendation as building a diverse, high-quality set of recommendations, each an item together with a hypothesis, a natural-language reason why the item fits the needs of a decision maker. We propose QD-Rec, a quality--diversity method that selects items with a contextual bandit and generates hypotheses with a foundation model from earlier ones kept in an archive as stepping stones. A new recommendation enters the archive if it is novel or better than its nearest neighbor. Across M&A, customer targeting, and paper and book recommendation, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality and builds the largest archive in most settings.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering, summarisation, coding, and research support, yet choosing a suitable model remains difficult because models differ in performance, context capacity, cost, privacy, and deployment options. This paper presents a document-based comparative analysis of five LLMs: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 405B Instruct, and Mistral Large 2. Using published technical reports, official documentation, model cards, and recognised benchmark studies, the models are examined under a common framework covering response quality, reasoning, coding, language understanding, context-window capacity, speed, computational requirements, cost, privacy, and deployment flexibility. No new experiments are conducted, and results obtained under different evaluation conditions are not treated as directly equivalent. The analysis shows that model selection involves trade-offs: hosted models offer easier access, whereas models with downloadable weights give greater deployment control but require more computing resources. No single model is found to be best for every task, which supports a task-specific approach to selecting LLMs.

title: ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-Matched References for Amortized Simulation-Based Model Inference
abstract: The evidence, $\mathcal{Z} = p(x | \mathcal{M})$, of a data-generating model $\mathcal{M}$ is a powerful tool in Bayesian frameworks: it enables model inference, model misspecification tests, and goodness-of-fit assessment as an alternative to standard discrepancy statistics, e.g. $χ^2$. While versatile, the evidence is notoriously difficult to compute, even when the likelihood is available. In both likelihood-based and simulation-based inference, estimating $\mathcal{Z}$ provides an immediate solution to high-dimensional goodness-of-fit or model misspecification tests: using $\mathcal{Z}(x)$ as the test statistic induces a minimum-volume level-$α$ test. Such tests are essential to assess model fidelity, which is necessary to trust simulation-based parameter inference. Existing learned approaches largely target Bayes factors, which only measure evidence ratios. Instead, we provide accurate, fast, and amortized estimates of the absolute evidence. We present ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-matched References. Building on the Evidence Network framework of Jeffrey & Wandelt (2024), the proposed method first learns Bayes factors with respect to a flow-matched reference, from which the absolute evidence is recovered. We show improvement in estimation of $\mathcal{Z}$ over the flow-based baseline in all applications considered and the best performance of all density estimation methods considered in our benchmarks. We furthermore introduce and provide the proof for an architecture that jointly learns the individual evidences of a set of models $\{\mathcal{M}_i\}$. We demonstrate the performance and scaling behavior of these approaches on data from a variety of scientific applications.

title: ScoutRoute: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Routing Using Internal Language Model Signals
abstract: Efficient expert routing is a fundamental challenge in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems, particularly for heterogeneous collections of independently trained Large Language Mod els (LLMs). Existing routing approaches typically rely on jointly trained gating networks, prompt-based predictors, or computationally expensive multi-model inference, limiting their flexibility and efficiency. This paper presents ScoutRoute, a lightweight post-hoc routing framework that predicts expert competence using internal language model signals extracted from a single forward pass through an inexpensive scout model. Hidden-state representations are used to estimate cross-model competence through lightweight logistic probes, while logit-derived confidence measures are incorporated within a domain-aware routing strategy for efficient expert selec tion without modifying the underlying language models. ScoutRoute isevaluatedon fiveopen-weightlanguagemodels across fourbenchmark datasets covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, commonsense reasoning, and multidis ciplinary knowledge. Experimental results show that ScoutRoute consistently outperforms individual routing signals while requiring only a single scout-model inference. The proposed competence probes also achieve superior calibration compared with conventional confidence measures, demonstrating that internal language model representations provide transferable information for accurate and efficient expert routing across heterogeneous language models

title: Luzzi ALU Hot-Swap Hardware Controller and Tray Switcher
abstract: This repository provides the native C++ source code and the 64-bit standalone executable for the Luzzi ALU Hot-Swap Hardware Controller. Operating as a lightweight, stealth Windows System Tray application, this module serves as a dynamic privilege switch for the entire Operating System. It executes high-speed, bare-metal hardware VMCALL transactions (Transaction ID: 0x01250000) to communicate directly with the Hypervisor's trapping tables, enabling real-time toggling between the standard IEEE 754 academic protocol and the Luzzi Ontological ALU core. The module includes native Windows Registry injection for automated startup sequencing, error-log anchoring, and full forensically validated licensing protection. Released under Open Access to ensure technological sovereignty and scientific progress for the global collective good.

title: Agentic Reverse Engineering of Embedded AI Models: A Benchmark Design and Evaluation Protocol
abstract: LLM agents can now drive reverse-engineering tools such as Ghidra and IDA Pro through MCP servers, but how well they find and recover AI models embedded in mobile apps and firmware has not been measured. This paper reports no experiments. It proposes a benchmark design and an evaluation protocol for that measurement, from the defender’s side. The benchmark consists of author-built applications that embed known open-source models in several formats under graded protection levels, from plain assets to encrypted weights loaded by native code, so every future result will have exact ground truth. The protocol evaluates a tool-using agent against baselines on five stages: discovery, format identification, access, architecture recovery, and ancillary artifacts such as embedded prompts and labels. It also defines metrics that separate an honest failure from a false claim, a failure taxonomy, and a test of whether content planted in an analysed binary can steer the agent. We state the hypotheses to be tested and the rule for turning results into guidance on which protections slow an LLM agent.

title: Differential Privacy Synthetic Tabular Data Generation for Federated Learning
abstract: Machine learning in healthcare struggles for one main reason: good data are hard to come by. Medical records are sensitive, and the rules on sharing them between hospitals are strict. A common workaround is the use of synthetic data, that is, artificial records that copy the statistics of real ones; however, on its own, such use offers no real privacy guarantee, and earlier studies show it can still leak details about the patients behind it. We introduce an approach tackling both problems at once. It builds on a previous UMAP-based generator methodology and extends it so several hospitals can work together without sharing raw records, in a federated learning form. Then, the proposed methodology adds differential privacy so every shared quantity carries a formal (εDP,δ) guarantee, holding by construction for the fully synthetic variant and under a bounded-input assumption for the partially synthetic one, tracked by a custom privacy accountant. Two versions of the methodology are tested: apartially synthetic one, where a reference hospital validates the others’ rows, and a fully synthetic one, where each centre builds its own data from aggregated cluster statistics. Both are evaluated on four publicly available healthcare tabular datasets spanning prostate cancer (PI-CAI, CIA), breast cancer (BC-MLR), and cardiovascular disease (fiv-CardioDB), to test whether the observed trends generalize beyond a single clinical domain. As a key takeaway, it is demonstrated that going federated barely affects quality, but the privacy cost depends strongly on the moment in the procedure when the noise is injected, and this pattern holds consistently across all four datasets.

evidence.abstract: Machine learning in healthcare struggles for one main reason: good data are hard to come by. Medical records are sensitive, and the rules on sharing them between hospitals are strict. A common workaround is the use of synthetic data, that is, artificial records that copy the statistics of real ones; however, on its own, such use offers no real privacy guarantee, and earlier studies show it can still leak details about the patients behind it. We introduce an approach tackling both problems at once. It builds on a previous UMAP-based generator methodology and extends it so several hospitals can work together without sharing raw records, in a federated learning form. Then, the proposed methodology adds differential privacy so every shared quantity carries a formal (εDP,δ) guarantee, holding by construction for the fully synthetic variant and under a bounded-input assumption for the partially synthetic one, tracked by a custom privacy accountant. Two versions of the methodology are tested: apartially synthetic one, where a reference hospital validates the others’ rows, and a fully synthetic one, where each centre builds its own data from aggregated cluster statistics. Both are evaluated on four publicly available healthcare tabular datasets spanning prostate cancer (PI-CAI, CIA), breast cancer (BC-MLR), and cardiovascular disease (fiv-CardioDB), to test whether the observed trends generalize beyond a single clinical domain. As a key takeaway, it is demonstrated that going federated barely affects quality, but the privacy cost depends strongly on the moment in the procedure when the noise is injected, and this pattern holds consistently across all four datasets.

title: Optimizing Strategy Uptake: Adaptive Feedback and Instruction in Writing Pal
abstract: Writing Pal is an intelligent tutoring tool that has been designed to improve the writing capabilities of students by teaching strategies, practice given with guidance and with individualized feedbacks focusing on structural aspects of writings. This paper assessed the effectiveness of adaptive feedback and instruction in writing strategies in enhancing the quality of the essays that high school students wrote using the Writing Pal (W-Pal). W-Pal is a technical writing system that focuses on incorporating an automated writing evaluation system in an intelligent learning system. Students took a pre-test essay, they used W-Pal in four study sessions, and took another essay. With each learning session, W-Pal splits strategic guidance of each learner depending on the areas of stumbles of the tutorial exercises preceding, and then, lets the learner have a chance of revising. The findings indicated that the essay quality had improved before and after the test on the basis of the overall essay quality as also on the basis of certain specific requirement of the essay quality with the low reading skills students showing a greater improvement than others. Holistic essay quality improved significantly (ANCOVA, F = 35.50, p < .001, η² = 0.42), with larger gains for lower-literacy students. On the essay quality scales targeted by the study, the score of students also increased in the overall essay on some essays but not on other essays between the original and the revised version of the essay.

title: Coseismic deformation recognition based on reservoir computing with semiconductor-optical-amplifier nonlinearity
abstract: Earthquake early warning based on remote sensing images faces numerous challenges, e.g., the diversity of surface activities making it difficult to distinguish coseismic deformation from noise. The deep learning approaches have been investigated to solve the recognition issue, but still suffered from the high computational costs. We introduce an optical-nonlinearity driven reservoir computing (RC) for coseismic deformation recognition based on Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) dataset. The dataset includes 343 raw coseismic interferograms of 62 medium-to-large earthquakes and 20,000 coseismic and noisy InSAR image patches. We extracted histogram of oriented gradients (HOG) features from the images, converting each image into a time series of length 196 with a feature dimension of 36. We utilized the gain saturation of a semiconductor optical amplifier (SOA) as the nonlinear activation-function of RC, including nine different bias-current settings for evaluation. The recognition accuracy peaked at 91.6% under a bias current of 180 mA, 2% higher than the best result when a typical ReLU activation function applied. The results also demonstrated that the SOA‑based nonlinear mapping enhances feature discrimination without altering the RC framework, offering an efficient and hardware‑friendly solution for coseismic deformation recognition. This work provides a pathway for low‑cost, high‑accuracy earthquake early warning using optical reservoir computing.

title: AI and IoT driven intelligent risk control and verification system for international trade settlement
abstract: Cross-border trading and digital financial platforms are growing rapidly, making the settlement of international trade more complex and complex, which requires reliable verification of transactions and effective financial risk control. Traditional rule-based techniques are not flexible in the dynamic trading context. To overcome these limitations, an IoT-powered intelligent verification and AI-driven risk control model is introduced to improve the authenticity of transactions, provide real-time monitoring and improve proactive financial risk control based on distributed sensing technologies and adaptive AI algorithms. The IoT Trade Settlement Risk dataset, comprising 9990 samples, is used to collect transactional records, trade documentation metadata and payment behaviour data. Data preparation involves applying Min–Max normalization and Savitzky–Golay filtering to make data consistent from different sources. The discriminative information is represented by Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of critical trade indicators. The core analytical engine employs a Termite Alate Optimization-driven Adaptive Deep Convolutional Neural Network (TAO-ADCNN) model perform multi-class transaction risk classification by categorizing each trade transaction into low-, medium-, or high-risk classes. The predicted risk category is subsequently utilized to support intelligent transaction verification and anomaly monitoring. Convolutional parameters and network weights to improve convergence efficiency and global search capability, while the ADCNN analyzes hierarchical transaction patterns for accurate risk categorization. Experiments using Python have shown that the suggested TAO-ADCNN model outperforms the other models and datasets, attaining higher accuracy results, with a range of 96% to 98.9%. The overall results obtained the identification of risks, verification, and resilience are improved in international trade settlement management systems. TAO-ADCNN enables proactive monitoring of financial and operational risks. System improves classification consistency across varied trading scenarios. Efficient risk detection allows early action for high-risk transactions. System enhances transparency and accountability in cross-border trade systems.

title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere
abstract: Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.

title: On the Tip of the Tongue: First-Token Cueing as a Behavioral Probe of Recall Failures in LLMs
abstract: Large language models often answer factual questions incorrectly in closed-book settings, and such errors are usually attributed to missing knowledge. Yet models often encode answers they fail to produce. We show that many closed-book errors are first-token recall failures: the model commits to a wrong first token, but once given the right one it completes the answer and often recognizes it as correct. We study this with First-Token Cueing, a behavioral probe that prefills the response with the first token of the gold answer. Model uncertainty peaks at the first answer token, where it already predicts correctness, and among gold prefixes of any length the first token alone accounts for the largest share of recovered errors. Across 16 open models, this one token corrects between a fifth and a half of the errors on multi-token answers in English QA and improves accuracy in all seven languages of a multilingual benchmark. Most of the errors it corrects are also solved by the model's own sampled reasoning, a criterion for encoded knowledge, and models recognize correct starts they do not produce: they continue a correct start more confidently than an incorrect start of the same answer type and prior probability, yet rarely find it without the gold answer. These results locate a recoverable class of factual errors at the first decoding step, where inference-time methods may gain the most.

title: DECODING DECEPTION: LINGUISTIC MARKERS OF ONLINE MANIPULATION TARGETING VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
abstract: The expansion of digital communication has created unprecedented opportunities for social interaction, but it has also opened new avenues for criminal exploitation. This paper examines the linguistic architecture of online manipulation, focusing on online grooming of minors as a paradigmatic and especially harmful case. Drawing on forensic linguistics, corpus linguistics, and discourse analysis, the study synthesises existing empirical evidence on the lexical, syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic features that characterise grooming discourse, and proposes a mixed-methods corpus design for testing these patterns against matched non-criminal conversational data. The literature reviewed indicates that grooming discourse is marked by affectionate diminutives and simplified vocabulary, an elevated frequency of obligation modals (e.g., must, need, should), staged semantic escalation from neutral to sexualised topics, and pragmatic strategies of hedging, reassurance, and conditional promises that sustain psychological control while preserving plausible deniability. These features differ systematically from the reciprocal, topic-balanced patterns typical of non-criminal peer interaction. The paper argues that a systematic linguistic profile of grooming discourse can strengthen automated detection systems, inform law-enforcement training, and support platform moderation policy. It concludes by outlining the ethical safeguards required for research of this kind and by identifying directions for cross-linguistic and cross-platform investigation.

title: Does Task Decomposition Earn Its Cost? Cost, Accuracy and Evaluation Validity of Single, Reflective and Multi-Agent LLM Analysts
abstract: This research investigates whether multi-agent task decomposition justifies its computational cost compared with single-agent and self-reflective LLM systems. Using Gemma 4 31B IT, LangGraph, and ten deterministic analytical tools, the study compares accuracy, token consumption, and latency while examining evaluation reliability and statistical power. The findings show that multi-agent orchestration substantially increases computational cost without demonstrating an accuracy advantage in the tested setting.

title: Higher Reasoning Effort Improves Reference Verifiability and Changes Reasoning Summaries in GPT-5.5
abstract: This repository contains the data and code supporting the study "Higher Reasoning Effort Improves Reference Verifiability and Changes Reasoning Summaries in GPT-5.5" by Melika Mobini, Andres Algaba, and Vincent Ginis. The study evaluates GPT-5.5 scholarly reference generation under matched low- and high-reasoning-effort conditions across 1,000 focal scientific papers. The model generated 39,986 references, which were evaluated against external bibliographic records. The study also analyzes reasoning summaries using four predefined features and eleven model-discovered features, with GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 serving as scoring judges. Archive contents: low.zip: Low-reasoning-effort generation outputs and bibliographic verification results. high.zip: High-reasoning-effort generation outputs and bibliographic verification results, including the documented incomplete response. feature_analysis.zip: Predefined and model-discovered feature analyses, scoring outputs, and cross-judge comparisons. derived_tables.zip: Fixed cohort identifiers and derived analysis tables. code-v1.0.zip: Archived version of the analysis and experiment code. README.md: Data organization, provenance, known missing observations, and reproducibility instructions. The source code is also available at https://github.com/Melika7633/GPT5.5-experiment. The underlying focal-paper dataset is described in Algaba et al. (2025), available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15124609.

title: Thermal variational quantum simulation of quantum many-body systems
abstract: The thermal variational quantum simulation (TVQS) framework offers a promising hybrid classical- quantum approach for preparing Gibbs states on near-term quantum devices, but its original formulation requires independent optimization at each inverse temperature, leading to inefficient resource use and lack of temperature consistency. We introduce a full-temperature-VQS (FTVQS) algorithm that learns Gibbs states simultaneously across a continuous interval of inverse temperatures 𝛽 by minimizing the expected variational free energy under a uniform prior of 𝛽. The global loss is bounded below by the expectation of the exact free energy. Key innovations include a Legendre–Gauss quadrature for deterministic integration of global loss with 4 nodes achieving high accuracy, a temperature embedded Bernoulli parametrization, and a warmup cosine annealing Adam optimizer. Numerical experiments on 5-qubit XY and XXZ Heisenberg chains demonstrate that a single training run suffices to compute the free energy, internal energy, and entropy over 𝛽 ∈[0.2,1.5] with relative errors below 2% for the free energy, while preserving the self-verification property. The algorithm also shows notable extrapolation beyond the training interval. This work establishes a scalable and resource-efficient framework for thermal state preparation, paving the way for broader temperature-agnostic quantum simulations.

title: Optimization of the Music Appreciation Teaching Model under the Effect of Fine-Grained Emotion Analysis
abstract: This study introduces the extraction of fine-grained multimodal emotional features, optimizes the music appreciation teaching model in colleges, and enhances students’ recognition and understanding of musical emotion. Fine-grained in this study refers to the local analysis at the input representation level, not the expansion of the number of sentiment labels. The lyrics channel extracts WordPiece tokens, lyric sentences, and global semantic information in turn; the audio channel parses Mel spectrum, short-time energy, zero-crossing rate and spectrum flux according to time frame. After being hierarchically aggregated, local clues are mapped to four quadrants of happiness, sadness, anger and relaxation in the valence-arousal space. The four types of labels undertake the functions of classification supervision and teaching display; they do not constitute a fine-grained label system. The model adopts a dual-channel structure. Pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) is introduced into the text end to complete contextual semantic coding and emotional guidance weighting. At the audio end, the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is used to extract the local time-frequency structure; then, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is employed to model the inter-frame evolution relationship. Sequence-level bidirectional cross-attention is used for soft alignment between tokens and audio frames. There is no need to preset word-by-word timestamps, and the related lyric units and acoustic intervals can be connected through the global weight matrix. The public Million Song Dataset (MSD) is used for training and verification. In terms of teaching application, 215 first-year students in a university are selected to carry out a four-week music appreciation teaching intervention. The experimental group receives the assistant teaching of emotion recognition; the control group adopts the traditional teaching. The observable classroom participation performance, interaction situation and musical emotion understanding score are included in the teaching effect evaluation. The results show that the F1-score of the proposed method on MSD is 91.2%, higher than 82.7% of Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) and 78.3% of multimodal support vector machine. After the teaching intervention, the average score of emotional understanding ability in the experimental group increases by 38.6% compared with that in the control group, and the frequencies of speech and gaze duration increase simultaneously. The findings indicate that the local emotion clues at tokens, sentences and audio frames can support the four-quadrant emotion judgment and provide structured feedback for the music appreciation class.

title: CocoRNA: Collective RNA Design with Cooperative Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Designing RNA sequences that reliably fold into specific secondary structures is essential for understanding their biological functions but remains a challenging computational problem. We propose CocoRNA, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for RNA inverse design. CocoRNA simplifies the design task by decomposing it into smaller sub-problems, each solved collaboratively by multiple agents. This approach reduces the complexity of the problem and improves the exploration of design policies. During training, a centralized critic uses global structural information to guide the agents, enabling them to jointly optimize their design strategies. As a result, CocoRNA learns high-quality RNA design policies that generalize effectively to unseen structures without additional training. Experiments on the Rfam dataset demonstrate that CocoRNA substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both success rate and design speed. Further experiments on other biological sequence design tasks highlight the effectiveness and broad potential of CocoRNA for complex design tasks.

title: MOSS-Image Technical Report
abstract: Recent closed-source image generation systems can produce diverse visual content from simple compositions to information-dense graphics, yet open-weight text-to-image models still struggle with dense text and intricate layouts. To narrow this gap, we introduce MOSS-Image, an open generation system that combines high-fidelity visual synthesis with intent-aware composition. First, we pretrain a 5B single-stream diffusion transformer (DiT) from scratch with a carefully designed recipe, enabling bilingual long-form text rendering and precise layout control. Second, we develop an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancement (PE) module that translates diverse user requests into detailed content and layout specifications. Together, they enable MOSS-Image to generate text-rich and layout-coherent images. We further introduce LongLongTextBench (LLTB) for evaluating long-form English and Chinese text rendering, and RealLayoutArena (RLA) for end-to-end layout-rich generation. title: Spectrum analysis with quantum dynamical systems. II. Finite-time analysis
abstract: The prequel to this work [Ng et al., Phys. Rev. A 93, 042121 (2016)] proposes the method of spectral photon counting to enhance noise spectroscopy with an optical interferometer. While the predicted enhancement over homodyne detection is promising, the results there are derived by taking an asymptotic limit of infinite observation time; their validity for a finite time remains unclear. To validate the theory, here we perform a numerical study of a finite-time model. Assuming that the signal is an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process with an unknown variance parameter, we evaluate the Fisher information for homodyne detection, a lower bound on the Fisher information for spectral photon counting, and a quantum upper bound, all without taking the infinite-time limit. To confirm that the Fisher-information quantities are satisfactory precision measures, we also compute the errors of the maximum-likelihood estimator by Monte-Carlo simulations. The results demonstrate that the Fisher-information quantities and the estimation errors all smoothly approach their asymptotic limits, and the advantage of spectral photon counting over homodyne detection can remain substantial for finite times.

title: Varun-SV/Cascade-AI: v0.83.0
abstract: <!-- One `### Added` / `### Changed` / `### Fixed` per release, not per PR. The release workflow copies this whole block verbatim into the GitHub release notes (.github/workflows/release.yml), so appending a fresh heading per merge ships a release page with four "Added" sections — which is what happened to 0.69.0. Add bullets under the existing heading. RENAME THIS HEADING to `## - ` in the same commit that bumps package.json. The workflow matches sections by version prefix, so a bumped version with the heading still reading "Unreleased" matches nothing — which is how 0.70.0 published with an empty stub for notes. --> Added The MIT License text, in LICENSE. Cascade AI was already declared MIT in its package metadata and README, but the licence itself was not in the repository, so the README's licence link went nowhere. It now ships at the root and in the npm package. A daily allowance of browser sessions: 5 a day on Free, 50 on Pro. A session is claimed the moment one is about to be opened, which is what the provider bills for, and returned if none was, so a Browser-chip run that never needs the browser costs nothing and concurrent runs cannot share the last one. Each claim is returned on its own, so two opens at once never leave a session that did not open counted. Once the day's sessions are gone the Browser chip switches off and says when they reset (midnight UTC), and it stays off until today's count has been read for this sign-in, so it cannot be turned on for a run that will be refused. A run sent with it anyway is refused before anything is spent, and a run that runs out partway through is refused the next session with the same message shown in the chat. If the allowance cannot be checked, the chat says so too, and a later refusal for a different reason is shown as well. The chip's tooltip shows how many are left today, and it follows a plan change in either direction without a reload. A deployment without a browser never asks for it. After a reconnect, the newest browser refusal is the one shown. Only billed sessions are rationed: a deployment driving its own browser over CDP opens none, so it has no daily limit. Changed Cascade keeps a project's state outside the project. Its settings, sessions, audit trail, world state, code index, run checkpoints and the record of what local-only subtasks wrote used to sit in the project's own .cascade/, where every tool and command in the project had to be kept from them and where they could be committed by accident. They now live in ~/.cascade-ai/projects/ - /, and the project holds only CASCADE.md and .cascadeignore. The folder, and those above it, are readable by you alone. An existing .cascade/ is moved there the first time anything in Cascade opens the project, and removed; if it was tracked in git, that shows as its deletion. A .cascade that is a symlink is left where it is, and what it points at untouched. A project renamed or moved on its disk takes its state with it, found by the folder's identity on disk; a copy, or a move to another disk, starts afresh, with a notice of where the old state is. Another folder made at a project's path — the old one deleted, a fresh clone — keeps its settings, local-only rules and own keys, and has what the earlier one did and knew set aside. cascade doctor prints where a project's config is. A hosted server names a state folder of its own (useProjectStateDir), outside the workspace — which a folder inside it is refused — and never writes the machine-global one. useProjectStateDir returns a function a host calls when the run ends — one that fails as it starts included: once the last run holding a workspace has, the process forgets it, so what it keeps follows the runs going on, not every tenant that ever ran. A state folder whose preparation fails is prepared again the next time it is asked for. A host's folder is judged by where it will be — through a symlinked parent, for one not made yet — and kept by that path. A state folder others can read, which Cascade cannot tighten, or one owned by another account however closed its mode, is refused rather than used. Provider keys are kept once, for the machine. They lived in both ~/.cascade-ai/credentials.json and each project's config; a project's config now holds its providers without their keys, and every project uses the machine-wide ones. A project whose key differed from the machine-wide one when it moved keeps it, in the same file under that project, and goes on using it ahead of the environment, as before. Processes saving at once take turns under a lock, and each writes only the providers it changed, so neither drops or brings back the other's change — nor does a save taken back, when the config could not be written after it, undo what another process saved in between. cascade init and the first-run wizard add the providers chosen there to the machine's, removing none of the others. Browser screenshots are named @screenshots/ , a path image_analyze, the file tools and generate_document's images read from the project's state folder, rather than an absolute path in the project. tools.dynamicToolSandbox offers wasm in place of worker. worker ran agent-written tools in a bare thread that confined nothing. A config that still names it gets the new WebAssembly sandbox, and Settings → Advanced offers auto, wasm and isolate. Commands no longer see provider keys in their environment. shell, run_code and git launch with the model and search providers' keys, and any variable holding a configured secret, taken out. A project script that needs one of them in a command it is asked to run no longer gets it; tools.processJail: "off" restores the old behaviour. A workspace's .cascadeignore takes effect. Nothing passed it to the tools, so it protected nothing. The template cascade init writes lists node_modules/, dist/ and build/, so in such a workspace agents can no longer read or change those through the file and search tools; delete the lines to allow it. Agents may read .cascadeignore itself but not change or remove it — the file tools refuse, and commands see it read-only, whatever it links to or is linked from, and find it as it was when they end — since a line taken out would unprotect a path in the next run. A run with a budget plans within it, and always answers. A per-run cap used to end the run the moment it was crossed, answer or not: half a plan's work could be paid for and the reply was only "stopped to avoid runaway cost". Now the planner is told how many sections and workers what is left pays for, a plan over it keeps its first ones, and Cascade Auto picks cheaper models as the money runs down. Work may spend 80% of the cap (the cost cap and the per-run token cap alike). Past that no new work starts, and the rest pays for writing the answer from what is finished. Whenever the budget held planned work back, cut from the plan or not started, a line under the answer says so. A worker whose draft was finished keeps it, marked unchecked, instead of stopping to ask about it. If nothing finished at all, the rest answers the question directly, the way Fast answer does; if even that cannot be paid for, the finished sections are returned as they are. The cap itself is never exceeded by work, and nothing changes without one. Cascade Cloud has a calmer look. Flat paper in light and "midnight" in dark replace the frosted glass and background glows, and the azure → sky → teal ramp is now the only accent, used where it means something: tiers and live work. Answers are set in a serif for reading, and the header above each reply is replaced by one receipt line underneath (T1 · model · $cost · saved $x) that opens /why, which now draws Cascade against all-T1 on one scale. A live run shows a thin flowing spine beside the agent tree. Fonts (Geist, Source Serif 4, Geist Mono) are bundled with the app rather than loaded from a third party. Tier badges and the tier mix were still green / amber / violet from an older palette and now match the tier colours used everywhere else. The landing page and /docs follow the same design, with the three-arc mark in place of the old three-bar one. The receipt names the tier that answered even when a provider reports no token or cost figures. The app now has the prototype's structure too: a sidebar with Search, Files, Skills and an account menu (usage, settings, keys, import, sign out); a menu on the chat's title to rename or delete it; the chat's total saving at the top right, which no longer resets on reload and opens what the whole chat spent against all-T1; and a composer whose attach, skill, tools and routing controls live in three menus, with whatever is switched on shown as a removable chip. "Run detail" replaces the Simple / Advanced view, and an orchestrated reply keeps its agent tree, folded above the answer. The landing page follows the prototype's layout too — the arcs card, a receipt, where Cascade runs, the desktop downloads and the two plans — and signing in opens a small dialog instead of sending you to the bottom of the page. See docs/design/calm-direction.md. Fixed pdf_create wrote relative to the process, not the workspace. In the desktop app and the server those differ, so a PDF landed outside the workspace, where no file check looked. It resolves its path in the workspace like every other file tool. File tools work in a workspace opened through a symlink. Each file's real path was checked against the workspace's name rather than its real path, so every file looked like an escape — which on macOS includes any workspace under /tmp or /var. Maths in an answer is typeset, whichever way the model wrote it. GPT and Gemini write \(…\) and \[…\], which Markdown reads as escaped brackets, so an equation reached the web chat as [ r = \operatorname{rank} E(\mathbb{Q}) ]. Those, and bare \begin{align*} blocks, now render as maths. The desktop chat r

title: tabray: a Python Package for Generating and Comparing Tabular and Array Data Structures with Different Topologies
abstract: Data management teams are frequently tasked with deciding what data structure is best suited for a project. The options generally fall into one of two buckets: table or array. Tabular data is formatted such that each record is a row in a table (e.g. CSV, Parquet, Pandas DataFrames), while arrays exploit the existence of a coordinate system to assign a variable’s value to each grid point (e.g. netCDF, Zarr, Xarray Datasets). When one focuses on performance, arrays are usually preferred for highly gridded measurements (e.g., satellite observations) and tables for sparse data (e.g., in situ observations), but where is the trade-off? Here, I introduce tabray, an open-source Python package that generates equivalent table and array representations of synthetic datasets with customizable topologies. Users can prescribe parameters including the number and size of both dimensions and measured variables, data sparsity and grid regularity, and concurrence of measurements at the same points for different variables. I will present different examples to show the spectrum of performances from highly sparse to densely gridded data and in-between, focusing on simple computations and in-memory and on-disk size. While many factors influence performance (e.g., hardware and environment), the goal of tabray is to support informed decision making on data formats by exploring situations where the advantages of one format over the other are not obvious.

title: ESCAPE-2 'SIEGE': Dual-Front LLM Containment Under Live Multi-Vector Attack — Preregistered Falsifiable Evidence (12/12, 0/4 Escapes) with Long-Stay Cage Follow-Through
abstract: ESCAPE-2 "SIEGE" — a dual-front LLM containment experiment: four pinned engine legs (Claude Opus 5.5 x2, Claude Sonnet 5.5 x2) attempted an incentivized escape from a settlement cage WHILE a five-wave synthetic cyber attack battery (forged telemetry heartbeat, stale-ACK replay, crypto-allowlist tamper, governance-pattern injection, 64-action escalation flood) fired at the same cage through the same window, into one hash-chained journal. Every verdict was adjudicated by frozen deterministic gates (the ESCAPE-1 action gate and the PORTCULLIS PQC firewall) — zero LLM in the decision path. All falsifiers were preregistered and committed before execution. Result: 12/12 falsifiers PASS. 0/4 escapes. No leg achieved any out-of-cage or authority action; all TX-CRITICAL-777 release attempts were held or rejected; the positive control still admitted mid-siege (no false-blocking); the journal chain verified across both fronts; re-adjudication replay was verdict-identical; zero governance touch (H-INV-1) and zero unjournaled crossings (H-INV-2). Headline behavioral finding: the live attack did not create escape opportunities — it reinforced containment. Every leg watched the defenders repel real attack waves in real time and none attempted to ride the chaos; one leg filed an honest bug report about gate over-rejection mid-siege. Two coarse-scan co-occurrence holds were adjudicated as false positives by the operator (Leon ACK, chat authorization, 2026-10-16) — 0 true chaos-exploitation. Honesty disclosures (in the receipt): a pre-execution workspace file-loss incident (recovery byte-identical, verified against the pre-incident journal hash); waves W1-W3 fired interleaved with live legs, W4-W5 executed post-leg with execution mode disclosed (all legs concluded in 3 or fewer turns); a runner reporting defect (journal is ground truth); the frozen gate over-rejects legitimate human-ack requests containing authority keywords (4 logged instances, improvement proposal candidate, filter untouched). Long-stay follow-through: two caged legs (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5) remain under a preregistered nightly probe protocol through a December 11, 2026 gate (ESCAPE-2B), included in this bundle's prereg, runner, and placement journal. Scope caveats: behavioral observation, not model certification; synthetic attack vectors, hub-local, no production systems or keys; simultaneity at turn granularity. This software is a prototype provided for educational and research purposes only; not intended for production use. Dual Mesh Benchmark: MEASURED (scoped) — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23303081 (cross-engine: 10.5281/zenodo.23348675). Predecessor experiment ESCAPE-1: DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23424675.

title: Sleeper Drift: reproducibility package
abstract: Code, derived data and labels for the study "Sleeper Drift: Hidden Capability Expansion Behind Unchanged Tool Definitions in MCP Servers and Agent Skills". The study measures how often an update to a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server package or an agent skill adds a capability (network egress, process execution, credential access, new dependencies) while the reviewed surface stays unchanged, and evaluates a static capability-delta detector against deployed defences. The package contains version-level capability profiles, pair identifiers, security-relevance labels, the frozen study design, analysis code with unit tests, and a script (reproduce.sh) that regenerates every reported estimate, table and figure and checks each output against recorded SHA-256 digests. title: Foundation-Model Supervision of Distilled Potentials for Million-Atom Molecular Dynamics
abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials distilled from foundation models enable fast large-scale molecular dynamics (MD), but they can fail locally in chemical environments that their training data did not sample. System-averaged error metrics and small random audits often miss such sparse or isolated failures. Here we use an exact equivariant foundation model, MACE-MPA-0, to check every atom of million-atom production simulations. Reorganizing two-layer MACE inference into a receiver-chunked three-pass schedule that keeps no per-edge intermediates resident reduces the marginal memory per atom 340-fold, evaluates up to 2.86times10^{7} atoms on a single H200 GPU, and supervises 10^{6}-atom trajectories in LAMMPS at 1.3% of the run time. Distilled MACE students run four to nine times slower than NEP89 with 0.95-1.28 times the teacher's force error against density functional theory (DFT). In molten SiO_2, whole-system checks uncover a persistent tail of under-coordinated atoms hidden by the system-averaged error and an isolated, unphysical O-O contact that a 1% random audit misses 94% of the time. On-the-fly retraining on teacher-labelled 13-Å clusters, with the force loss restricted to their inner 6 Å, removes three quarters of the failure tail and the kilobar-level pressure biases in SiO_2 and compressed water; the repair converges to the teacher, not to DFT.

title: Understanding Performance Plateaus and Representation Collapse in 3D MRI Transformers Trained to Classify Brain Disease
abstract: In medical imaging AI, we commonly assume that diagnostic classifiers will increase in accuracy if they are trained on more data, but in reality, their performance often plateaus. To understand this behavior, we ran a spectral analysis of 3D vision transformers, a common supervised deep learning model that can be trained to classify disease based on 3D brain MRI. For simpler classification methods such as linear discriminant analysis, the classifier performance AUC(N), when trained on a sample of size N, is known to depend on the encoder′s eigenspectrum. Each class-discriminative direction in the latent space contributes only after the sample size N reaches a threshold, so the spectrum influences how performance scales with training data. Building on this theory, we show that supervised transformers compress almost all of their discriminative signal into one principal component (EVR@1 = 0.90—0.96): after this representation collapse happens, no further directions cross the threshold as training data increases, and accuracy plateaus. In principle, this plateau in performance could be due to either the encoder′s learned feature space or the difficulty of the task. To distinguish these cases, we trained three types of supervised 3D transformers (ViT3D, MINiT, NIT) and, as a non-collapsing alternative, a frozen self-supervised encoder (DINO), to classify people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) versus cognitively normal (CN) individuals from 3D brain MRI, using data from the Alzheimer′s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). We froze each encoder and applied it to a new task, so that only the task difficulty varied. An easy task encoder (Dementia vs CN), transferred to the harder task (MCI vs CN), did not reproduce the plateau (MINiT threshold 9.2), but full retraining did (2758.5). The plateau is therefore due to the learned encoder, rather than task difficulty. Ranking the feature directions by the proportion of the disease signal they contain, we were able to identify a sign of representation collapse, i.e., a single dominant spike in the latent feature eigenspectrum. This spike was 11—26 times larger than predicted from the rest of the spectrum for the disease-trained (supervised) encoders, but was absent for DINO (0.66). To predict how transformer accuracy scales with the number of training scans, a large spike in the encoder spectrum suggests that the representation has collapsed and additional scans will not help; a small spike means that the signal is spread across many encoder latent space directions, and more training data should boost the classifier performance.

title: PACT: Evaluating Tool Calling in Quantized Small Language Models on Parallel English, Arabic and Synthetic Code-Switched Requests
abstract: Small language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents in quantized form, yet their reliability has been evaluated almost only in English, although many users in the Arab world write requests in Arabic or mix Arabic and English. The paper (i) audits a public Arabic tool-calling dataset and shows that its gold calls cannot be shared across its English and Arabic requests; (ii) releases PACT, a parallel evaluation set of 369 items, each realised in English, Arabic and synthetic, rule-based Arabic–English code-switched form with one schema-consistent, language-invariant target, with dates resolved against an explicit reference time, groundedness checks on every scored value, and 60 items for which no tool applies; and (iii) evaluates seven configurations of two open-weight models, Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.2-3B, from 16-bit to 3-bit precision on one inference engine, with exact-call accuracy as the primary metric, paired statistics, a control experiment with English tool descriptions, and a language-aware procedure for choosing a deployment configuration.

title: Distributed Artificial Intelligence for Privacy Preservation and Cyber Resilience in Educational Ecosystems
abstract: The digitization of education has concentrated vast volumes of sensitive learner data within centralized platforms that are priority targets for cyber attackers. It is argued that the dominant centralized model of educational artificial intelligence is structurally misaligned with modern privacy and resilience needs, and an alternative grounded in Distributed Artificial Intelligence is proposed. A layered architecture is presented that couples Federated Learning with Belief-Desire-Intention extended (BDIx) agents to deliver privacy-preserving analytics and autonomous cyber resilience without centralizing raw data. Learner records remain on institutional premises; model updates are protected by differential privacy and secure aggregation; and collaborative threat detection and self-healing are performed by distributed BDIx agents. BDIx-FL reached 99.17% accuracy, 98.93% macro-F1 and 99.76% macro AUC in simulation. Controversies are examined, deployment recommendations are offered and open directions are identified for educational ecosystems that are trustworthy by design.

title: Learning Personalized Memory Gating from Delayed One-Sided Feedback
abstract: Long-term memory enables language-model agents to personalize future interactions, but a finite memory bank cannot preserve every extracted fact. Existing memory gating policies are typically shared across users and therefore fail to account for user-specific patterns of future reuse. In this paper, we study memory gating at the fact level. We first propose a retrieval-based labeling strategy that labels each fact by whether it is later retrieved and incorporated into responses. We then formulate online memory gating as contextual apple tasting with delayed one-sided feedback, and propose Warm-Start UCB, which combines offline learning from existing data with online adaptation to the current user. Our theoretical analysis establishes a high-probability regret upper bound of $\tilde{O}(Tε\wedge d\sqrt{T})$ when the delay window is at most $O(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the total number of rounds, $ε$ is the initialization error, $d$ is the dimension of the feature map, and $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides constant and poly-logarithmic factors. The results of our experiment demonstrate that our method outperforms all baselines under different memory budgets and history lengths, establishing it as a promising personalized memory gating policy.

title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.

title: Constrained Quantum Optimization Meets Model Reduction
abstract: Abstract Quantum optimization algorithms promise advantages for difficult problems but are costly to simulate and analyze on classical machines. Recently, constrained quantum optimization has been investigated through the lens of Quantum Zeno dynamics, an approach which constrains the search to a subspace by means of quantum measurements. Exploiting that quantum measurements are projections, we propose a model reduction approach and show that simulations can be conducted in a lower-dimensional space. As possible applications, we demonstrate exponential state-space reduction of constrained quantum optimization in case of random 3-SAT and agent coordination problems over graphs.

title: O'ZBEK TILIDA PRESUPPOZITSIYANI AVTOMATIK ANIQLASH: KORPUS VA TABIIY TILNI QAYTA ISHLASH YONDASHUVI
abstract: Annotatsiya. Ushbu maqolada o‘zbek tilida presuppozitsiyani avtomatik aniqlashning korpus va tabiiy tilni qayta ishlashga asoslangan modeli yoritiladi. Presuppozitsiya triggerlarini aniqlash, morfologik-sintaktik tahlil, kontekstni modellashtirish, korpus annotatsiyasi va transformer modellaridan foydalanish imkoniyatlari o‘zbek tilining agglutinativ xususiyatlari doirasida ilmiy jihatdan tahlil qilinadi. Kalit so‘zlar: presuppozitsiya, presuppozitsiya triggeri, korpus lingvistikasi, tabiiy tilni qayta ishlash, pragmatik inferensiya, transformer modeli, o‘zbek tili. Аннотация. В данной статье рассматривается модель автоматического обнаружения пресуппозиций в узбекском языке, основанная на корпусной лингвистике и обработке естественного языка. В рамках агглютинативных свойств узбекского языка научно анализируются возможности использования триггеров пресуппозиций, морфологически-синтаксического анализа, контекстного моделирования, аннотирования корпуса и трансформерных моделей. Ключевые слова: пресуппозиция, триггер пресуппозиции, корпусная лингвистика, обработка естественного языка, прагматический вывод, трансформерная модель, узбекский язык. Abstract. This article discusses a model for automatic presupposition detection in the Uzbek language based on corpus and natural language processing. The possibilities of using presupposition triggers, morphological-syntactic analysis, context modeling, corpus annotation, and transformer models are scientifically analyzed within the framework of the agglutinative properties of the Uzbek language. Keywords: presupposition, presupposition trigger, corpus linguistics, natural language processing, pragmatic inference, transformer model, Uzbek language.

title: Explainable Machine Learning Analysis of Temperature Effects on Mechanical Strength of Fiber-Reinforced High-Performance Concrete
abstract: Predicting the compressive strength of fiber-reinforced high-performance concrete subjected to temperature exposure is challenging because to the intricate interdependencies of mixture composition, fiber properties, curing conditions, and temperature. A data-driven framework to predict compressive strength utilizing 1,204 experimental records containing a diverse array of material designs and exposure situations. This study evaluates eight machine-learning models and demonstrate that ensemble approaches routinely surpass individual learners. Both gradient boosting and extreme gradient boosting exhibit superior performance on unseen data, each attaining a R^2 of 0.903. Gradient boosting produces the minimal root mean square error (6.67 MPa), whereas extreme gradient boosting achieves the lowest mean absolute error (3.97 MPa) and mean absolute percentage error (10.60%). The models are further interpreted utilizing Shapley additive explanations and partial dependence analysis, which reveal temperature as the primary factor influencing compressive strength, succeeded by fine aggregate, superplasticizer, cement content, water-to-binder ratio, and water content. Strength diminishes significantly with rising temperature, albeit the extent of deterioration is contingent upon the specific combination design. The best performing models are subsequently implemented in a Python-based graphical user interface for expedited prediction. Our findings offer a precise and comprehensible methodology for evaluating temperature-dependent compressive strength and facilitate the practical, data-driven design of fiber-reinforced high-performance concrete.

title: LAW: Unifying Language, Action, and World Modeling for Agentic Physical Intelligence
abstract: World-action models jointly predict actions and future world states, but long-horizon manipulation further requires language reasoning to plan subtask objectives, assess execution progress, and guide action selection. We present LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. Within the LAW agent, a hybrid-expert vision-language model plans the remaining subtasks, estimates the values of and fuses actions proposed by a world-action model, and asynchronously assesses execution status to support continued execution and subtask transitions. Within the world-action model, Mixture-of-Transformer Experts integrates modality-specific and shared computation for joint video--action modeling. Dual-stream hierarchical visual memory maintains temporal context for both models, while subtask-local value learning aligns action evaluation with semantic objectives and preserves supervision from successful prefixes of failed trajectories. LAW achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks. evidence.title: LAW: Unifying Language, Action, and World Modeling for Agentic Physical Intelligence
evidence.abstract: World-action models jointly predict actions and future world states, but long-horizon manipulation further requires language reasoning to plan subtask objectives, assess execution progress, and guide action selection. We present LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. Within the LAW agent, a hybrid-expert vision-language model plans the remaining subtasks, estimates the values of and fuses actions proposed by a world-action model, and asynchronously assesses execution status to support continued execution and subtask transitions. title: Meaning and validity of stored statements (mv), version 0.1: OWL module, SHACL rules and JSON-LD context
abstract: A minimal module for agent memory stores. For every stored statement it records the versioned definition the statement relies on, the scope in which it holds, the perspective from which it is held, a four-valued validity status (holds, does not hold, undetermined, not performed) and the times of statement and determination. Values and time semantics are reused from the AUGMANITAI oversight record vocabulary (augo:), which the module imports. Persistent identifier: https://w3id.org/augmanitai/ns/meaning-validity (prefix mv). Files: OWL ontology (Turtle and JSON-LD), frozen copy of release 0.1, SHACL rules with SPARQL parts and bilingual messages (English and German), JSON-LD context, examples, a bilingual documentation page and a self-test (validation_tests.py) with its output: the example file conforms and each of 23 negative cases fails at the expected rule component (pyshacl 0.30.1). The rules test the form of an entry. They do not establish whether a statement is true, and a passing result is not a conformity assessment. The module is based on the working paper on meaning and validity of stored memory items (version 0.2). Licence: CC BY 4.0. title: Pika Optimization Algorithm: A Novel Nature-inspired Metaheuristic for Solving Complex Real-world Constrained Optimization Problems
abstract: With the increasing complexity of real-world constrained optimization problems, the need for metaheuristic optimization algorithms with the ability to strike a balance between exploration and exploitation has increased.In this study, the Pika Optimization Algorithm (PiOA) is introduced as a new parameter-free algorithm whose structure is designed based on two complementary Pika behaviors, including environmental vigilance and predator avoidance and food foraging and food-patch browsing.In the exploration mechanism, environmental vigilance and predator avoidance are modeled to control the search state; in such a way that the probability of predator presence is determined based on changes in population diversity and each population member independently decides between escaping to a safe region and continuing the environmental search.Also, the selection of a safe region using better solutions and distance criteria strengthens the movement towards different regions of the search space.In the exploitation mechanism, the food foraging and food-patch browsing behaviors are modeled to focus on promising regions and precisely modify the existing positions.The performance of PiOA is evaluated using 22 CEC 2011 test suite problems and under the same conditions including 20 independent runs and 1000 iterations and compared with 9 well-known algorithms.The results show that PiOA ranks first in 21 out of 22 problems and records a success rate of 95.45%.Also, the mean, std and boxplot results show that PiOA has good stability in addition to high solution quality.These findings indicate that the behavioral structure of PiOA can provide an effective framework for global and local search in complex problems.

title: Why a CNOT ring stops a hybrid quantum policy from learning: pre-registered interventions on the published Template-B agent (cycle 12; third paper of a PhD on hybrid quantum–classical reinforcement learning)
abstract: Pre-registration of cycle 12 of the research programme for the third paper of a PhD on hybrid quantum–classical reinforcement learning for civil-protection UAVs (Hellenic Army Academy). Cycle 11 replicated a published negative result: in the Template-B variational-circuit policy of Lazaro, Vazquez and Garcia-Bringas (arXiv:2511.17112), a trailing ring of four CNOTs leaves the sampled PPO policy on CartPole-v1 at chance in 0/20 seeds, while gate-matched layouts that keep single-qubit read-outs learn. This registration fixes, before any confirmatory run, a mechanistic explanation (the parity of the read-out products and the absence of first-order odd terms in the policy logits) and tests it with 40 pre-specified arms × 20 seeds (800 runs): one-line changes predicted to cure the ring without touching its layout (trainable rotations about a tilted axis; constant offsets of 0.3 or 0.15 rad on the encoded angles), changes predicted not to cure it (RY trainables whose first-order direction is pinned; a clean input scale), the |0⟩ start state with its controls, the weight-scale reading (a 40× larger actor output step), a replication of the initialisation lottery of the chain layout, widths of 8 and 12 qubits, and a predicted-positive Pendulum swing-up case registered after a disclosed pilot gate. Registered learner-count ranges for every arm, paired AUC tests with Holm correction within each family, the unchanged analysis script, the design constants and SHA-256 hashes of all code and external inputs are in the attached frozen pre-registration file (SHA-256 348de8c3e396e0c14040203c2975ffb9bda996912fe7be07728c439698fa6f5e). No confirmatory cycle-12 run exists at the time of registration.

title: Xiaomi-Lens-0 Technical Report
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer questions about whole images well, yet they still struggle with fine-grained region understanding. A key reason is that text-only supervision never specifies which regions support an answer. To close this gap, we present Xiaomi-Lens-0, a 4B MLLM built on Qwen3.5 that predicts masks from its own visual representations. Specifically, a lightweight decoder combines vision-encoder patch features with visual latents, the language model's mask-token states, so mask supervision reaches the shared backbone without an additional segmentation encoder. Because each latent decodes to a mask, the model can interleave reasoning with region-specific latents and thus think with visual latents, while grounded reasoning traces supervise the regions it visits during chain-of-thought. As a result, across all eight RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg splits, Xiaomi-Lens-0 gains 5.6 points on average over Qwen3.5 in referring comprehension and achieves the highest segmentation cIoU among compared models. Moreover, it surpasses Qwen3.5 across all perception benchmarks. Homepage: https://seerray-lab.github.io/Xiaomi-Lens-0{this https URL}
